claim: The proteolytic cleavage site in rat α2δ-1 is between A and V in the sequence LEA//VEM.
source: We identified the proteolytic cleavage site in rat α2δ-1 to be between A and V in the sequence LEA//VEM, by homology with the published data in rabbit (Jay et al., 1991; De Jongh et al., 1990) (Figure 1a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published data in rabbit and reference to Figure 1a,b.

claim: The cleavage site sequence LEA//VEM is strongly conserved in mammals.
source: This sequence is strongly conserved in mammals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing sequence conservation.

claim: Transient expression of wild type α2δ-1 in cell lines results in only partial cleavage into α2 and δ subunits.
source: Transient expression in cell lines of wild type (WT) α2δ-1 resulted in only partial cleavage into α2 and δ subunits, clearly observed only following deglycosylation (Figure 1c, lanes 1 and 3), compared to the complete proteolytic cleavage observed in brain (Figure 1c, lanes 2 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1c comparing cell line expression to brain tissue.

claim: α2δ-1 is completely proteolytically cleaved in brain.
source: Transient expression in cell lines of wild type (WT) α2δ-1 resulted in only partial cleavage into α2 and δ subunits, clearly observed only following deglycosylation (Figure 1c, lanes 1 and 3), compared to the complete proteolytic cleavage observed in brain (Figure 1c, lanes 2 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1c comparing brain tissue to cell line expression.

claim: Replacing LEAVEM in α2δ-1 with a hexavaline (V6) sequence completely prevents proteolytic processing.
source: Replacing LEAVEM in α2δ-1 with a hexavaline (V6) sequence (Figure 1b) completely prevented its proteolytic processing, as shown by the absence of cleaved α2-1 on reducing gels of whole cell lysate (WCL) (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1d demonstrating absence of cleaved α2-1.

claim: The lack of proteolytic cleavage does not affect the ability of α2(V6)δ-1 to bind 3H-gabapentin.
source: However, we found that the lack of proteolytic cleavage did not affect the ability of α2(V6)δ-1 to bind 3H-gabapentin (Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1e demonstrating gabapentin binding.

claim: α2(V6)δ-1 is concentrated in detergent-resistant membranes (DRMs) like wild-type α2δ-1.
source: Furthermore, the α2(V6)δ-1, like wild-type (WT) α2δ-1, was found to be concentrated in detergent-resistant membranes (DRMs; Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and the KD for 3H-gabapentin binding in DRMs was unchanged, being 76.2 ± 7.8 nM for WT α2δ-1 and 85.0 ± 13.7 nM for α2(V6)δ-1 (Figure 1e), indicating that the uncleaved pro-form of α2δ-1 is likely to be correctly folded.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 demonstrating DRM localization.

claim: The KD for 3H-gabapentin binding in DRMs is 76.2 ± 7.8 nM for WT α2δ-1.
source: Furthermore, the α2(V6)δ-1, like wild-type (WT) α2δ-1, was found to be concentrated in detergent-resistant membranes (DRMs; Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and the KD for 3H-gabapentin binding in DRMs was unchanged, being 76.2 ± 7.8 nM for WT α2δ-1 and 85.0 ± 13.7 nM for α2(V6)δ-1 (Figure 1e), indicating that the uncleaved pro-form of α2δ-1 is likely to be correctly folded.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurement of KD values.

claim: The KD for 3H-gabapentin binding in DRMs is 85.0 ± 13.7 nM for α2(V6)δ-1.
source: Furthermore, the α2(V6)δ-1, like wild-type (WT) α2δ-1, was found to be concentrated in detergent-resistant membranes (DRMs; Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and the KD for 3H-gabapentin binding in DRMs was unchanged, being 76.2 ± 7.8 nM for WT α2δ-1 and 85.0 ± 13.7 nM for α2(V6)δ-1 (Figure 1e), indicating that the uncleaved pro-form of α2δ-1 is likely to be correctly folded.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurement of KD values.

claim: The uncleaved pro-form of α2δ-1 is likely to be correctly folded.
source: Furthermore, the α2(V6)δ-1, like wild-type (WT) α2δ-1, was found to be concentrated in detergent-resistant membranes (DRMs; Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and the KD for 3H-gabapentin binding in DRMs was unchanged, being 76.2 ± 7.8 nM for WT α2δ-1 and 85.0 ± 13.7 nM for α2(V6)δ-1 (Figure 1e), indicating that the uncleaved pro-form of α2δ-1 is likely to be correctly folded.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that uncleaved α2(V6)δ-1 binds gabapentin with similar affinity and localizes to DRMs like WT α2δ-1.

claim: Insertion of a Human Rhinovirus (HRV) 3C-protease site into α2δ-1 in place of the endogenous cleavage motif completely prevents proteolytic cleavage.
source: We then decided to control the proteolytic processing of α2δ-1 by inserting a Human Rhinovirus (HRV) 3C-protease site (Cordingley et al., 1990) into α2δ-1, in place of the endogenous cleavage motif, to form α2(3C)δ-1 (Figure 1b). This substitution completely prevented its proteolytic cleavage (Figure 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation and data shown in Figure 1f demonstrating absence of cleavage.

claim: α2(3C)δ-1 is expressed on the cell surface at similar levels to WT α2δ-1.
source: However, α2(3C)δ-1 was still expressed on the cell surface (Figure 1f–i) and in DRMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), at similar levels to WT α2δ-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1f-i and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: α2(3C)δ-1 is localized in DRMs at similar levels to WT α2δ-1.
source: However, α2(3C)δ-1 was still expressed on the cell surface (Figure 1f–i) and in DRMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), at similar levels to WT α2δ-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The amount of proteolytically-processed α2δ-1 is increased on the cell surface compared to the whole cell lysate in transfected tsA-201 cells.
source: We have previously shown that the amount of proteolytically-processed α2δ-1 is increased on the cell surface compared to the WCL in transfected tsA-201 cells (Kadurin et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Proteolytic processing of α2δ-1 is not essential for its trafficking to the plasma membrane.
source: However, the present results show that this processing of α2δ-1 is not essential for its trafficking to the plasma membrane.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that uncleaved α2(3C)δ-1 reaches the cell surface.

claim: Co-expression of WT α2δ-1 results in an enhancement of CaV2.2/β1b currents in heterologous systems.
source: It has previously been established that co-expression of WT α2δ-1 results in an enhancement of CaV2.2/β1b currents in heterologous systems (for review see [Dolphin, 2012]).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review.

claim: WT α2δ-1 produces an 8.6-fold increase of CaV2.2/β1b currents at +10 mV.
source: We could confirm this result using β1b-GFP to ensure that all cells examined contain β1b; WT α2δ-1 produced an 8.6-fold increase of CaV2.2/β1b currents at +10 mV (Figure 2a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: α2(3C)δ-1 does not increase CaV2.2/β1b currents when co-expressed.
source: Strikingly, no increase was observed when α2(3C)δ-1 was co-expressed with CaV2.2/β1b (Figure 2a,b; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2a,b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: α2(V6)δ-1 is unable to increase CaV2.2 currents.
source: In agreement with this, another uncleavable construct used, α2(V6)δ-1, was also unable to increase CaV2.2 currents (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: CaV2.2 co-immunoprecipitates with α2(3C)δ-1 to the same extent as WT α2δ-1.
source: We next examined whether α2(3C)δ-1 is impaired in its interaction with CaV2.2, which would explain its inability to increase CaV2.2 currents. However, we found that CaV2.2 co-immunoprecipitates with α2(3C)δ-1 to the same extent as WT α2δ-1 (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2c demonstrating co-immunoprecipitation.

claim: In undifferentiated N2A cells, uncleaved α2(3C)δ-1 increases the cell surface density of CaV2.2 channels by 123% compared to CaV2.2/β1b alone.
source: Furthermore, using extracellularly-tagged CaV2.2 to quantify the channels inserted into the plasma membrane (Cassidy et al., 2014), we found that in undifferentiated N2A cells, the uncleaved α2(3C)δ-1 remains capable of increasing the cell surface density of CaV2.2 channels (123% increase compared to CaV2.2/β1b alone), by a similar extent to WT α2δ-1 (140% increase; Figure 2d,e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2d,e and citation to methodology.

claim: In undifferentiated N2A cells, WT α2δ-1 increases the cell surface density of CaV2.2 channels by 140% compared to CaV2.2/β1b alone.
source: Furthermore, using extracellularly-tagged CaV2.2 to quantify the channels inserted into the plasma membrane (Cassidy et al., 2014), we found that in undifferentiated N2A cells, the uncleaved α2(3C)δ-1 remains capable of increasing the cell surface density of CaV2.2 channels (123% increase compared to CaV2.2/β1b alone), by a similar extent to WT α2δ-1 (140% increase; Figure 2d,e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2d,e and citation to methodology.

claim: α2(3C)δ-1 increases cell surface expression of CaV2.2 in tsA-201 cells.
source: α2(3C)δ-1 also increased cell surface expression of CaV2.2 in the tsA-201 cells used for electrophysiology (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Co-expression of TASK3 hyperpolarizes the membrane potential of N2A cells.
source: We therefore co-expressed the leak K+ channel, TASK3 (Kim et al., 2000), to hyperpolarize their membrane potential (Figure 2f), in order to determine whether this would differentially affect CaV2.2 trafficking supported by WT α2δ-1 and α2(3C)δ-1.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2f and citation.

claim: Hyperpolarization of N2A cells by TASK3 does not differentially affect CaV2.2 trafficking supported by WT α2δ-1 and α2(3C)δ-1.
source: We therefore co-expressed the leak K+ channel, TASK3 (Kim et al., 2000), to hyperpolarize their membrane potential (Figure 2f), in order to determine whether this would differentially affect CaV2.2 trafficking supported by WT α2δ-1 and α2(3C)δ-1. This was not the case, as a similar increase in CaV2.2 surface expression was observed in the presence of TASK3 for CaV2.2, with either WT α2δ-1 or α2(3C)δ-1 (Figure 2g).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: When heterologously expressed in cell lines, α2(3C)δ-1 causes an increase of CaV2.2 surface expression but does not result in an increase of CaV2.2 currents.
source: Thus, when heterologously expressed in cell lines, α2(3C)δ-1 cause an increase of CaV2.2 surface expression, but does not result in an increase of CaV2.2 currents (see cartoon in Figure 2h), strongly suggesting α2(3C)δ-1 may play an inhibitory role on CaV2.2 function.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the data and reference to Figure 2h.

claim: α2(3C)δ-1 may play an inhibitory role on CaV2.2 function.
source: Thus, when heterologously expressed in cell lines, α2(3C)δ-1 cause an increase of CaV2.2 surface expression, but does not result in an increase of CaV2.2 currents (see cartoon in Figure 2h), strongly suggesting α2(3C)δ-1 may play an inhibitory role on CaV2.2 function.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that α2(3C)δ-1 increases surface expression but not currents.

claim: Co-expression of ER-lumen-targeted 3C-protease with α2(3C)δ-1 results in efficient proteolytic cleavage of α2(3C)δ-1 into α2 and δ.
source: In order to determine whether α2(3C)δ-1 could be cleaved at the inserted 3C-protease site, we then co-expressed an ER-lumen-targeted 3C-protease together with α2(3C)δ-1 (Figure 3a). This resulted in efficient proteolytic cleavage of α2(3C)δ-1 into α2 and δ, as shown by the appearance of a band of the size of the α2 moiety, which reached the cell surface (Figure 3b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Co-expression of an inactive form of 3C-protease with a mutation in the catalytic site (C147V) does not affect α2(3C)δ-1.
source: As expected, co-expression of an inactive form of 3C-protease with a mutation in the catalytic site (C147V) failed to affect α2(3C)δ-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Proteolytic cleavage by 3C-protease restores CaV2.2 currents through channels containing α2(3C)δ-1 subunits.
source: Next we addressed the important question of whether proteolytic cleavage by 3C-protease could restore the currents through CaV2.2 channels containing α2(3C)δ-1 subunits. In order to do this, we co-expressed 3C-protease with CaV2.2/β1b/α2(3C)δ-1, and found that α2δ-1-mediated CaV2.2 current enhancement was robustly rescued by the active protease, whereas the inactive mutant 3C-protease (C147V) had no effect (Figure 3c–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3c-e.

claim: The inactive mutant 3C-protease (C147V) has no effect on CaV2.2 currents when co-expressed with α2(3C)δ-1.
source: Next we addressed the important question of whether proteolytic cleavage by 3C-protease could restore the currents through CaV2.2 channels containing α2(3C)δ-1 subunits. In order to do this, we co-expressed 3C-protease with CaV2.2/β1b/α2(3C)δ-1, and found that α2δ-1-mediated CaV2.2 current enhancement was robustly rescued by the active protease, whereas the inactive mutant 3C-protease (C147V) had no effect (Figure 3c–e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3c-e.

claim: Proteolytic cleavage by 3C-protease is not accompanied by any change in CaV2.2 trafficking.
source: This was not accompanied by any change in CaV2.2 trafficking (Figure 3f,g).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3f,g.

claim: The peak IBa increase due to the 3C-protease is 5.4-fold at +10 mV, compared to inactive protease.
source: The peak IBa increase due to the 3C-protease was 5.4-fold at +10 mV, compared to inactive protease (Figure 3c,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3c,d.

claim: Co-expression of 3C-protease with α2(3C)δ-1 results in an increased activation rate of the CaV2.2 currents, to the same extent as WT α2δ-1.
source: Co-expression of 3C-protease with α2(3C)δ-1 also resulted in an increased activation rate of the CaV2.2 currents, to the same extent as WT α2δ-1 (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: When α2(3C)δ-1 is not present, there is no increase in CaV2.2 currents attributable to 3C-protease.
source: As expected, when α2(3C)δ-1 was not present, there was no increase in CaV2.2 currents attributable to 3C-protease (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of active 3C-protease results in cleavage of α2(3C)δ-1 and rescues enhancement of CaV2.2 currents by α2(3C)δ-1, without any effect on trafficking.
source: In summary, expression of active, but not the inactive form of 3C-protease results in cleavage of α2(3C)δ-1 and rescues enhancement of CaV2.2 currents by α2(3C)δ-1, without any effect on trafficking, providing evidence that proteolytic processing of α2δ-1 is required to promote voltage-dependent activation CaV2.2 channels.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings and provides evidence for the conclusion.

claim: Proteolytic processing of α2δ-1 is required to promote voltage-dependent activation of CaV2.2 channels.
source: In summary, expression of active, but not the inactive form of 3C-protease results in cleavage of α2(3C)δ-1 and rescues enhancement of CaV2.2 currents by α2(3C)δ-1, without any effect on trafficking, providing evidence that proteolytic processing of α2δ-1 is required to promote voltage-dependent activation CaV2.2 channels.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: α2δ-3 contains an incomplete MIDAS motif in its VWA domain.
source: In order to further distinguish between the effects of α2δ subunits on CaV2.2 channel trafficking and voltage-dependent activation, we also examined the behavior of α2δ-3, because we surmised it might have a less prominent trafficking effect, as it contains an incomplete MIDAS motif (Whittaker and Hynes, 2002) in its VWA domain, which we have shown is essential for the trafficking and function of α2δ-1 and α2δ-2 (Hoppa et al., 2012; Cassidy et al., 2014; Canti et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work.

claim: The MIDAS motif is essential for the trafficking and function of α2δ-1 and α2δ-2.
source: In order to further distinguish between the effects of α2δ subunits on CaV2.2 channel trafficking and voltage-dependent activation, we also examined the behavior of α2δ-3, because we surmised it might have a less prominent trafficking effect, as it contains an incomplete MIDAS motif (Whittaker and Hynes, 2002) in its VWA domain, which we have shown is essential for the trafficking and function of α2δ-1 and α2δ-2 (Hoppa et al., 2012; Cassidy et al., 2014; Canti et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: α2δ-3 produces a much smaller increase (31%) than α2δ-1 (~140%) on CaV2.2 cell surface expression.
source: Indeed, we found that α2δ-3 produced a much smaller increase than α2δ-1 (31%, compared to ~140%) on CaV2.2 cell surface expression (Figure 4a,b), which we attribute to the absence of a complete MIDAS motif in α2δ-3 (Whittaker and Hynes, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4a,b and citation.

claim: The smaller effect of α2δ-3 on CaV2.2 cell surface expression is attributed to the absence of a complete MIDAS motif in α2δ-3.
source: Indeed, we found that α2δ-3 produced a much smaller increase than α2δ-1 (31%, compared to ~140%) on CaV2.2 cell surface expression (Figure 4a,b), which we attribute to the absence of a complete MIDAS motif in α2δ-3 (Whittaker and Hynes, 2002).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data and citation.

claim: α2δ-3 is fully cleaved into α2 and δ in vivo.
source: The site of proteolytic cleavage in α2δ-3 has not been previously determined, although it is fully cleaved into α2 and δ in vivo (Davies et al., 2010), and enhances CaV2.2 currents (Davies et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: α2δ-3 enhances CaV2.2 currents.
source: The site of proteolytic cleavage in α2δ-3 has not been previously determined, although it is fully cleaved into α2 and δ in vivo (Davies et al., 2010), and enhances CaV2.2 currents (Davies et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A V6 mutation across the predicted cleavage site in α2δ-3 prevents proteolytic cleavage.
source: We therefore first identified a potential cleavage site in α2δ-3 by sequence alignment (Figure 4c), and then showed by mutational analysis that a V6 mutation across the predicted cleavage site prevented proteolytic cleavage, determined by the appearance of the δ-3 moiety in a reducing gel (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and also prevented the functional effects of α2δ-3 on CaV2.2 currents (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A V6 mutation across the predicted cleavage site in α2δ-3 prevents the functional effects of α2δ-3 on CaV2.2 currents.
source: We therefore first identified a potential cleavage site in α2δ-3 by sequence alignment (Figure 4c), and then showed by mutational analysis that a V6 mutation across the predicted cleavage site prevented proteolytic cleavage, determined by the appearance of the δ-3 moiety in a reducing gel (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and also prevented the functional effects of α2δ-3 on CaV2.2 currents (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to unpublished data.

claim: α2(3C)δ-3 is expressed on the cell surface to a similar extent to WT α2δ-3, despite the complete absence of proteolytic cleavage.
source: We then replaced this sequence in α2δ-3 with the HRV-3C motif, to form α2(3C)δ-3 (Figure 4c). We found that α2(3C)δ-3 was expressed on the cell surface to a similar extent to WT α2δ-3 (Figure 4d), despite the complete absence of proteolytic cleavage (Figure 4d, lane 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: When 3C-protease is co-expressed, α2(3C)δ-3 is almost completely cleaved at the inserted HRV-3C site.
source: Importantly, when the 3C-protease was co-expressed, we found that α2(3C)δ-3 was still present on the cell surface, and was almost completely cleaved at the inserted HRV-3C site (Figure 4d, lane 4), although this had no effect on WT α2δ-3 (Figure 4d,e; Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: 3C-protease has no effect on WT α2δ-3.
source: Importantly, when the 3C-protease was co-expressed, we found that α2(3C)δ-3 was still present on the cell surface, and was almost completely cleaved at the inserted HRV-3C site (Figure 4d, lane 4), although this had no effect on WT α2δ-3 (Figure 4d,e; Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4d,e and Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: α2(3C)δ-3 does not increase CaV2.2 currents.
source: As we also found for α2(3C)δ-1, α2(3C)δ-3 did not increase CaV2.2 currents, whereas WT α2δ-3 produced a 6.6-fold increase (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: WT α2δ-3 produces a 6.6-fold increase in CaV2.2 currents.
source: As we also found for α2(3C)δ-1, α2(3C)δ-3 did not increase CaV2.2 currents, whereas WT α2δ-3 produced a 6.6-fold increase (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Inducing proteolytic cleavage of α2(3C)δ-3 by 3C-protease substantially rescues the enhancement of CaV2.2 currents.
source: However, inducing proteolytic cleavage of α2(3C)δ-3 by 3C-protease substantially rescued the enhancement of CaV2.2 currents, whereas the mutant protease 3C (C147V) did not (Figure 4g,h).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4g,h.

claim: The mutant protease 3C (C147V) does not rescue the enhancement of CaV2.2 currents by α2(3C)δ-3.
source: However, inducing proteolytic cleavage of α2(3C)δ-3 by 3C-protease substantially rescued the enhancement of CaV2.2 currents, whereas the mutant protease 3C (C147V) did not (Figure 4g,h).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4g,h.

claim: The increase in peak IBa due to the 3C protease is 2.7-fold at +10 mV, compared to inactive protease, for α2(3C)δ-3.
source: The increase in peak IBa due to the 3C protease was 2.7-fold at +10 mV, compared to inactive protease.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurement.

claim: WT α2δ-3 has a much smaller effect on CaV2.2 cell surface trafficking than WT α2δ-1.
source: In summary WT α2δ-3 has a much smaller effect on CaV2.2 cell surface trafficking than WT α2δ-1, but proteolytic cleavage of α2(3C)δ-3 still produces a substantial increase in CaV2.2 currents.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: Proteolytic cleavage of α2(3C)δ-3 produces a substantial increase in CaV2.2 currents.
source: In summary WT α2δ-3 has a much smaller effect on CaV2.2 cell surface trafficking than WT α2δ-1, but proteolytic cleavage of α2(3C)δ-3 still produces a substantial increase in CaV2.2 currents.
evidence: The claim is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: Incubation of cells expressing α2(3C)δ-1 or α2(3C)δ-3 with purified 3C-protease does not result in their proteolytic cleavage at the plasma membrane.
source: In order to further probe the role of proteolytic processing of the α2δ subunits on calcium channel currents, independent of their trafficking effects, we next turned to application of extracellular protease. However, we found that incubation of cells expressing α2(3C)δ-1 or α2(3C)δ-3 with purified 3C-protease did not result in their proteolytic cleavage at the plasma membrane (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, and data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and reference to unpublished data.

claim: Extracellular thrombin does not cleave WT α2δ-3.
source: As an alternative approach, we inserted a thrombin cleavage site into α2δ-3 to produce α2(Th)δ-3 (Figure 5a,b). Importantly, we first showed that extracellular thrombin did not cleave WT α2δ-3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and we found that α2(Th)δ-3 reached the cell surface as an uncleaved protein (Figure 5c,d; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: α2(Th)δ-3 reaches the cell surface as an uncleaved protein.
source: As an alternative approach, we inserted a thrombin cleavage site into α2δ-3 to produce α2(Th)δ-3 (Figure 5a,b). Importantly, we first showed that extracellular thrombin did not cleave WT α2δ-3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and we found that α2(Th)δ-3 reached the cell surface as an uncleaved protein (Figure 5c,d; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5c,d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Application of thrombin in the extracellular medium produces marked cleavage of α2(Th)δ-3 on the cell surface.
source: Furthermore, application of thrombin in the extracellular medium then produced marked cleavage of α2(Th)δ-3 on the cell surface (Figure 5c), and the optimal incubation period was about 60 min (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The optimal incubation period for thrombin cleavage of α2(Th)δ-3 is about 60 min.
source: Furthermore, application of thrombin in the extracellular medium then produced marked cleavage of α2(Th)δ-3 on the cell surface (Figure 5c), and the optimal incubation period was about 60 min (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Uncleaved α2(Th)δ-3 fails to mediate CaV2.2 current enhancement.
source: In line with previous results, uncleaved α2(Th)δ-3 failed to mediate CaV2.2 current enhancement (Figure 5e).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: When thrombin is added to cells expressing CaV2.2/β1b and α2(Th)δ-3 prior to Ba2+ current recording, it results in an acute increase in IBa amplitude.
source: However, when thrombin was added to cells expressing CaV2.2/β1b and α2(Th)δ-3, prior to Ba2+ current recording, it resulted in an acute increase in IBa amplitude (Figure 5e–g), clearly demonstrating that cleavage of α2(Th)δ-3 has a direct effect to rescue CaV2.2/β1b/α2(Th)δ-3 currents.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5e-g.

claim: Cleavage of α2(Th)δ-3 has a direct effect to rescue CaV2.2/β1b/α2(Th)δ-3 currents.
source: However, when thrombin was added to cells expressing CaV2.2/β1b and α2(Th)δ-3, prior to Ba2+ current recording, it resulted in an acute increase in IBa amplitude (Figure 5e–g), clearly demonstrating that cleavage of α2(Th)δ-3 has a direct effect to rescue CaV2.2/β1b/α2(Th)δ-3 currents.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: When CaV2.2-HA is transfected with β1b and WT α2δ-1 into DRG neurons, there is a clear increase in CaV2.2-HA on the cell surface of the DRG cell bodies after 2 days, compared to CaV2.2-HA/β1b alone.

claim: WT α2δ-1 is essential for trafficking of CaV2.2 into the processes of hippocampal neurons.
source: In view of our finding that all endogenous α2δ-1 is proteolytically cleaved in axons but not cell bodies (Figure 6a), we then asked whether proteolytic processing was required for trafficking either of α2δ-1 itself, or of associated CaV2.2, into neuronal processes. For this purpose, we used cultured hippocampal neurons which can be transfected after the establishment of extensive neurite outgrowth in culture. We found the surprising result that, when we co-transfected CaV2.2/β1b with either WT α2δ-1, α2(3C)δ-1 or the corresponding empty vector, WT α2δ-1 was essential for trafficking of CaV2.2 into the processes of hippocampal neurons, whereas in the presence of α2(3C)δ-1, or without α2δ, there was virtually no trafficking of CaV2.2 out of the soma (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7a,b.

claim: In the presence of α2(3C)δ-1, or without α2δ, there is virtually no trafficking of CaV2.2 out of the soma in hippocampal neurons.
source: In view of our finding that all endogenous α2δ-1 is proteolytically cleaved in axons but not cell bodies (Figure 6a), we then asked whether proteolytic processing was required for trafficking either of α2δ-1 itself, or of associated CaV2.2, into neuronal processes. For this purpose, we used cultured hippocampal neurons which can be transfected after the establishment of extensive neurite outgrowth in culture. We found the surprising result that, when we co-transfected CaV2.2/β1b with either WT α2δ-1, α2(3C)δ-1 or the corresponding empty vector, WT α2δ-1 was essential for trafficking of CaV2.2 into the processes of hippocampal neurons, whereas in the presence of α2(3C)δ-1, or without α2δ, there was virtually no trafficking of CaV2.2 out of the soma (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7a,b.

claim: The inability of α2(3C)δ-1 to drive CaV2.2 into neuronal processes is reversed by co-expression of 3C-protease.
source: Strikingly, the inability of α2(3C)δ-1 to drive CaV2.2 into neuronal processes was reversed by co-expression of 3C-protease (Figure 7c,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7c,d.

claim: The failure of CaV2.2 to traffic into the neurites in the presence of α2(3C)δ-1 is not primarily due to a defect in the trafficking of the uncleaved α2δ subunit itself.
source: The failure of CaV2.2 to traffic into the neurites in the presence of α2(3C)δ-1 was not primarily due to a defect in the trafficking of the uncleaved α2δ subunit itself, since, when the α2δ subunits were transfected alone, WT α2δ-1 and α2(3C)δ-1 were both able to extensively access the hippocampal neurite compartment (Figure 7e,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7e,f.

claim: When α2δ subunits are transfected alone, WT α2δ-1 and α2(3C)δ-1 are both able to extensively access the hippocampal neurite compartment.
source: The failure of CaV2.2 to traffic into the neurites in the presence of α2(3C)δ-1 was not primarily due to a defect in the trafficking of the uncleaved α2δ subunit itself, since, when the α2δ subunits were transfected alone, WT α2δ-1 and α2(3C)δ-1 were both able to extensively access the hippocampal neurite compartment (Figure 7e,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7e,f.

claim: When co-transfected with CaV2.2/β1b, the trafficking of α2(3C)δ-1 into neurites is 37% lower than that of WT α2δ-1.
source: In contrast, when the localization of the α2δ subunits was examined following co-transfection with CaV2.2/β1b, the trafficking of α2(3C)δ-1 into neurites was 37% lower than that of WT α2δ-1 (Figure 7g,h), suggesting it has been retained by interaction with CaV2.2.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7g,h.

claim: α2(3C)δ-1 has been retained by interaction with CaV2.2.
source: In contrast, when the localization of the α2δ subunits was examined following co-transfection with CaV2.2/β1b, the trafficking of α2(3C)δ-1 into neurites was 37% lower than that of WT α2δ-1 (Figure 7g,h), suggesting it has been retained by interaction with CaV2.2.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the observation that α2(3C)δ-1 trafficking is reduced when co-expressed with CaV2.2.

claim: The association of CaV2.2 with mature processed α2δ subunits is essential for trafficking of the complex into hippocampal neurites.
source: Similar results to those with α2δ-1 were obtained when comparing the ability of WT α2δ-3 and α2(3C)δ-3 to traffic CaV2.2 into neurites, which was also reversed by 3C-protease (data not shown). This further confirmed that the association of CaV2.2 with mature processed α2δ subunits is essential for trafficking of the complex into hippocampal neurites (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and reference to unpublished data.

claim: The uncleaved α2(3C)δ-1 reduces Ca2+ entry in response to single AP stimulation in hippocampal boutons to 65.8 ± 9.1% of control.
source: We then examined the effect of expression of α2(3C)δ-1 alone in hippocampal neurons on action potential (AP)-induced Ca2+ entry into presynaptic boutons. These were identified by co-expressed vesicle-associated membrane protein-mOrange2 (VAMP-mOr2), and Ca2+ transients were measured using synaptophysin-GCaMP6f (sy-GCaMP6f, Figure 8a). The uncleaved α2(3C)δ-1 reduced Ca2+ entry in response to single AP stimulation in all experiments performed (Figure 8b,c), to 65.8 ± 9.1% (n = 7, p=0.0093, 1 sample t test) of control.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8a-c.

claim: The inhibitory effect of α2(3C)δ-1 on the response to a single AP is reversed by co-expression of 3C-protease.
source: The inhibitory effect of α2(3C)δ-1 on the response to a single AP was reversed by co-expression of 3C-protease in all experiments performed (Figure 8d,e), an increase of 81.5 ± 16.1% (n = 8, p<0.0001, 1 sample t test).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8d,e.

source: However, they have no effect on single channel conductance, and for CaV2 channels there are only minor effects of α2δ subunits on most parameters relating to open probability (Hoppa et al., 2012; Barclay et al., 2001; Brodbeck et al., 2002; Wakamori et al., 1999; Meir and Dolphin, 1998), which would be unlikely to account for the large increase in whole-cell conductance.
